372.title: The lamb (Exodus 12)
372.hook: blood on the doorposts, unleavened bread, eaten in haste; Christians call Jesus our Passover
372.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, Catholics light the paschal candle and hear the Exsultet, which calls Easter night the night of the true Lamb, and Exodus 12 is read every Holy Thursday at the Mass of the Lord's Supper.

segments.voice: Yesterday, let my people go: bricks without straw, nine plagues, and a heart that kept hardening. Your line was let my people go. Who did you remember among the workers you rarely see? Day three hundred seventy-two.

A meal eaten standing up. Belt fastened, sandals on, walking stick in hand, as if the car's running outside and you might have to leave mid-bite. Roast lamb, flat bread with no yeast because there's no time for dough to rise, bitter herbs. And outside, on the frame of the door, a smear of blood. That's the strangest dinner in the Bible, the night before Israel leaves Egypt. And its name is still in a Catholic church every Easter: on the tall candle, in the songs, in the word priests use for the whole mystery of Christ's death and rising.
screen: `A MEAL EATEN STANDING UP.` → `BLOOD ON THE DOOR FRAME.` → `A NAME STILL HEARD AT EASTER.`

segments.voice: First, the lamb. Each household takes a lamb, a year old, without blemish. On the fourteenth day of the month, at evening, they kill it, and with a bunch of hyssop they brush its blood on the two doorposts and the lintel. Then they eat it, roasted, with unleavened bread, in haste. Second, the night. This is the tenth plague, and the hardest page in Exodus: the death of the firstborn of Egypt. The text doesn't look away from the grief; it says there was a great cry in Egypt, with no house where there was not one dead. But where God sees the blood on the door, God passes over. In Hebrew the feast is called Pesach. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, calls it the Phase, that is, the Passage of the Lord. Third, the remembering. God says: this day shall be a memorial; you will keep it as a feast forever. And Jews still keep Passover every spring at the Seder table, telling this night to their children. Fourth, the word Catholics took from it: Pasch. In Latin and Greek, the same word, pascha, names both Passover and Easter. Jesus ate his last supper at Passover time, and John's Gospel places his death on the day of Preparation for the Passover, when the lambs were being made ready. Paul writes to the Corinthians: "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." At the Easter Vigil, the Easter Proclamation sings that this is the night the true Lamb is slain, whose blood marks the doorposts of believers. The paschal candle, the paschal mystery: every time a Catholic hears that word, it carries a lamb, a door, and a family eating in their traveling clothes.
screen: `A LAMB WITHOUT BLEMISH.` · `WHERE GOD SEES THE BLOOD, GOD PASSES OVER.` · `A MEMORIAL, KEPT FOREVER.` · `CHRIST OUR PASCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one meal with attention. If you have food in front of you, use these two minutes for it. If not, choose your next meal now and plan to slow it down. Look at what's on the plate before you begin. Where did it come from? Who grew it, carried it, cooked it? Take one bite and actually taste it. The Passover meal was eaten in a hurry, but every piece of it meant something, and people have been remembering it ever since. If you pray, you can give thanks before you eat, in your own way or in the Church's grace before meals. If you don't, simply give the food your full attention. The bell holds the time.
Pasch. From Hebrew Pesach, the Passover: the lamb, the blood on the door, the night of leaving. For Catholics, also Easter. Today's word.
Your line: the lord's passover. Today, at one meal, stop before the first bite and remember where it came from. Day three hundred seventy-two.

373.title: Through the sea (Exodus 14)
373.hook: the waters part and they walk through on dry ground
373.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, the reading of Israel's crossing of the sea in Exodus 14 is never omitted, and the Church's blessing of baptismal water recalls the people led dry-shod through the sea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pasch: a lamb, blood on the doorposts, bread eaten in haste. Your line was the lord's passover. Which meal did you slow down for? Day three hundred seventy-three.

They're out. After four hundred years, Israel walks out of Egypt with their dough still unrisen in the bowls. And within days, Pharaoh changes his mind again. What have we done, letting our labor go? He takes six hundred chosen chariots and every other chariot in Egypt and rides after them. The Israelites are camped by the sea. They look up and see the dust on the horizon. Water in front. Army behind. Nowhere to go. And they turn on Moses: weren't there enough graves in Egypt, that you brought us out here to die?
screen: `OUT OF EGYPT AT LAST.` → `CHARIOTS ON THE HORIZON.` → `WATER IN FRONT, ARMY BEHIND.`

segments.voice: First, Moses's answer to the people. Don't be afraid. Stand still and see what God will do. The Lord will fight for you, and you only have to keep quiet. Good advice, it sounds like. But then God says something surprising to Moses: why are you crying to me? "Speak to the children of Israel to go forward." Standing still was a start. It wasn't the end. Second, the night. The pillar of cloud that went ahead of them moves behind them, between Israel and Egypt, dark on one side and light on the other. Moses stretches his hand over the sea, and a strong east wind blows all night and turns the sea into dry land. The waters are divided, a wall on their right and on their left, and they walk through. Jewish tradition tells a story about this moment, a story people tell, not one in the text: that the sea didn't part until one man, Nahshon, walked in up to his neck. Third, the morning. The Egyptians follow, their chariot wheels clog, the waters come back. At dawn Israel sees the shore, and the text says the people feared the Lord, and believed. Fourth, what Catholics hear. Paul writes that the Israelites were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. That's why this reading is the one Old Testament reading at the Easter Vigil that may never be skipped. And when a priest blesses baptismal water, the prayer remembers the children of Abraham led dry-shod through the sea, a picture of everyone who will pass through the water of baptism.
screen: `STAND STILL. THEN: GO FORWARD.` · `A WIND ALL NIGHT, WALLS OF WATER.` · `DAWN: THEY FEARED, AND BELIEVED.` · `BAPTIZED IN THE CLOUD AND THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step through a fear. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing you're stuck in front of. A conversation, a diagnosis you haven't looked up, a form you haven't filled out, an apology. Notice the urge to stand still forever, waiting for the water to part on its own. For the first minute, be still; that's allowed. Then picture the very first step, the smallest possible one. Not the whole crossing. One step onto the wet sand. If you pray, you can listen for God's words to Moses: go forward. If you don't, just picture your foot moving. The bell holds the time.
Through the sea. Israel trapped between water and chariots, then walking through on dry ground, a crossing the Church reads as a picture of baptism. Today's word.
Your line: go forward. Today, take the first small step toward the thing you've been standing still in front of. Day three hundred seventy-three.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle scene from a movie.
what it means: a frightened people told to go forward, walking through death to freedom, a crossing Christians read as baptism.

374.title: Miriam's timbrel (Exodus 15:20–21)
374.hook: the prophetess leads the women in song and dance
374.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, after the reading of the crossing of the sea, Catholics sing the Song of Moses and Miriam from Exodus 15 as the responsorial psalm, and the same canticle is prayed in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, through the sea: water in front, chariots behind, and a word from God. Your line was go forward. What was your first step? Day three hundred seventy-four.

Think about who packs a drum when they're fleeing slavery in the middle of the night. You've got unrisen dough, your kids, whatever you can carry, a few minutes' notice. And somebody, more than one somebody, brings a hand drum. Then they cross the sea. They stand on the far shore, soaked and shaking, and look back at the water. And before anyone has worked out what to say, a woman picks up her drum, and the other women follow her out with their drums, dancing. Someone had planned for a celebration before there was anything to celebrate.
screen: `WHO PACKS A DRUM TO FLEE?` → `THE FAR SHORE.` → `A WOMAN PICKS UP HER DRUM.`

segments.voice: First, her name and her title. In the Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, the verse reads: "So Mary the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand." Mary. That's the same name. Miriam in Hebrew, Mariam in Greek, Maria in Latin. The mother of Jesus was named after this woman. And she's called a prophetess, the first woman in the Bible to get that title. Second, the timbrel. In Hebrew it's a tof, a hand drum, a round frame with skin stretched over it, held in one hand and struck with the other. Not a harp in a temple. A traveling instrument, made for dancing in the open. Third, the song. The chapter opens with a long song of Moses, eighteen verses of it. Then Miriam's is short, two lines, and she sings it back to the women: sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and its rider he has thrown into the sea. Some scholars think her short refrain may be one of the oldest pieces of poetry in the whole Bible, and that the longer song grew around it. Nobody can be sure. Fourth, where Catholics still sing it. At the Easter Vigil, right after the crossing of the sea is read, the people answer with this song: let us sing to the Lord, for he has covered himself in glory. And the Church prays it in the Liturgy of the Hours as a morning canticle. Miriam led the first song of freedom with a drum. Her namesake, Mary, would sing her own song of praise centuries later, about a God who lifts up the lowly.
screen: `MARY THE PROPHETESS, SISTER OF AARON.` · `A TOF: A HAND DRUM FOR DANCING.` · `TWO LINES, MAYBE THE OLDEST.` · `STILL SUNG AT THE EASTER VIGIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one line of praise. Yes, out loud, if you can, even quietly. Settle, and breathe. Choose a line you already know. A verse of a hymn, a refrain from Mass, the alleluia, a line from a psalm, or just a line of thanks in your own words set to any tune. Tap the rhythm on your knee or the table, like a drum. Sing it once. Then again, a little stronger. If you pray, let it be your praise for something you've come through. If you don't, let it be a song for anyone who made it to the far shore. The bell holds the time.
Miriam's timbrel. The hand drum of Miriam the prophetess, who led the women in song and dance on the far side of the sea. Today's word.
Your line: she led the song. Today, be the first to celebrate something good, out loud, before anyone else starts. Day three hundred seventy-four.

375.title: Manna (Exodus 16)
375.hook: bread every morning, just enough, and it spoils if hoarded
375.howItsDone: At Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, many parishes sing the versicle "You have given them bread from heaven," drawn from Wisdom 16:20, and Catholics pray for daily bread in the Our Father at every Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam's timbrel: a prophetess on the far shore, a hand drum, and the first song of freedom. Your line was she led the song. What did you celebrate out loud? Day three hundred seventy-five.

One month out of Egypt, the singing has stopped. They're in the desert, the food is gone, and the whole community starts complaining to Moses and Aaron. If only we'd died in Egypt, they say, where we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread till we were full. Notice how memory works. A month ago they were slaves making bricks without straw. Now Egypt is a buffet. Hunger rewrites the past fast. And God's answer to the complaining isn't a lecture. It's breakfast.
screen: `ONE MONTH OUT. NO FOOD.` → `IF ONLY WE'D DIED IN EGYPT.` → `GOD'S ANSWER IS BREAKFAST.`

segments.voice: First, the bread. In the morning, when the dew lifts, there's something on the ground, fine and flaky, like frost. The people look at it and say to each other, man hu, what is it? That question became its name: manna, the what-is-it. The text says it was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. Second, the rule. Gather what you need, about an omer a person, a few quarts. And the text says something strange: whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Moses says, leave none of it till morning. Some people do anyway, just in case. By morning it's crawling with worms and it stinks. Third, the rest. On the sixth day they gather double, and that portion keeps through the Sabbath. Some go out on the seventh day anyway, and find nothing. Bread for today, every day, for forty years. Fourth, where Catholics hear it. In John's Gospel, Jesus says the fathers ate manna in the desert, and then: I am the living bread come down from heaven. The Church sings it at Benediction before the Blessed Sacrament: you gave them bread from heaven, with all sweetness in it, words drawn from the Book of Wisdom. And in the Our Father, Matthew uses a Greek word for bread, epiousios, that appears almost nowhere else in all of Greek. Nobody knows exactly what it means. Daily? For tomorrow? The Douay-Rheims, following Saint Jerome's Latin, translates it supersubstantial bread. Many Catholics hear both at once: today's food, and the Eucharist.
screen: `MAN HU: WHAT IS IT?` · `ENOUGH, AND NO MORE.` · `HOARDED, IT SPOILS BY MORNING.` · `I AM THE LIVING BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask only for today's bread. Settle, and breathe. Notice what you're stockpiling in your head right now: tomorrow's worries, next month's bills, the argument you might have next week. That's the manna kept overnight. Set it down for two minutes. Then ask, simply, what do I need for today? Not for the year. For today. Enough food. Enough patience. Enough strength for one hard conversation. If you pray, you can use the line from the Our Father: give us this day our daily bread. If you don't, just name today's need and let tomorrow's wait. The bell holds the time.
Manna. From the Hebrew question man hu, what is it? Bread in the desert every morning, enough for one day. Today's word.
Your line: daily bread. Today, when a worry about next week shows up, ask instead what today needs, and do just that. Day three hundred seventy-five.

376.title: Arms held up (Exodus 17:8–13)
376.hook: when Moses tires, Aaron and Hur hold up his arms
376.howItsDone: At Mass, the priest prays the collect and the Eucharistic Prayer with arms raised and open, the ancient orans posture, and early Christian writers saw in Moses's outstretched arms a figure of the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna: bread every morning, enough for one day, and spoiled by morning if hoarded. Your line was daily bread. What did today actually need? Day three hundred seventy-six.

Try this, if you can, right where you are: lift both arms straight out and hold them there. The first ten seconds are easy. By thirty, your shoulders start to burn. By a minute, you're bargaining with yourself. Now imagine holding them up all afternoon, on a hilltop, in the desert sun, while below you a battle goes back and forth depending on whether your hands are up. That's Moses at a place called Rephidim. He's somewhere past eighty, if you follow the Bible's numbers. And his arms are getting heavy.
screen: `LIFT YOUR ARMS. HOLD THEM.` → `A HILLTOP AT REPHIDIM.` → `HIS ARMS GET HEAVY.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Amalek, a desert people, attacks Israel on the road. Moses tells a young man named Joshua to choose fighters and go out, and this is the first time Joshua appears in the Bible. Moses himself climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand, and two men go with him: his brother Aaron, and a man named Hur, about whom the Bible tells us almost nothing. Second, the strange rule of the battle. Whenever Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails. Whenever he lets them down, Amalek prevails. The text doesn't explain why. Third, the tiredness. Moses's hands grow heavy. He's not a superhero. So Aaron and Hur take a stone and put it under him, and he sits on it. Then they stand on either side, one on the left, one on the right, and hold up his hands. And the Hebrew word for how his hands stay, steady until the sun goes down, is emunah, the word that elsewhere means faithfulness, even faith. His hands were faithful because his friends held them. Fourth, what Christians saw. Very early, writers like Saint Justin Martyr looked at Moses with his arms stretched out wide and saw a figure of the cross: arms open, and the people saved. Catholics still see that posture every Sunday, when the priest raises his arms to pray the great prayers of the Mass on behalf of everyone there. And the story is honest that this was a battle; Exodus doesn't make war pretty. What it holds up is something smaller and very human: even Moses couldn't do it alone.
screen: `JOSHUA FIGHTS. MOSES CLIMBS.` · `HANDS UP, ISRAEL PREVAILS.` · `A STONE, AND A FRIEND ON EACH SIDE.` · `ARMS OUTSTRETCHED: A FIGURE OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold up someone who is tired. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose arms are getting heavy right now. A parent of a newborn. A friend caring for a sick spouse. A teacher at the end of the term. A priest or a nurse running on empty. You can't do their work for them. Aaron and Hur didn't fight the battle. But they could bring a stone, and stand on each side. What's your stone? A meal, a text, an afternoon of babysitting, a ride. If you pray, you can hold that person up before God. If you don't, just keep them in mind and choose one stone. The bell holds the time.
Arms held up. Moses's tired hands on the hilltop, held steady till sunset by Aaron and Hur, one on each side. Today's word.
Your line: hold up their arms. Today, bring one tired person their stone: something small that lets them sit down for a moment. Day three hundred seventy-six.

377.title: Sinai (Exodus 19)
377.hook: thunder, smoke, a trumpet, and a people told you shall be my own
377.howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that every baptized person shares in the common priesthood of the faithful, drawing on Exodus 19:6 and 1 Peter 2:9, and at Pentecost the Church remembers the Spirit coming with wind and fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arms held up: Moses on the hilltop, and two friends who held his hands steady till sunset. Your line was hold up their arms. Who did you bring a stone to? Day three hundred seventy-seven.

Three months out of Egypt, they come to a mountain in the desert and set up camp at its foot. It's the same mountain where Moses saw the bush burning. He'd been told back then: when you bring the people out, you'll worship God on this mountain. Now here they all are, a whole nation of former slaves, tents spread across the plain, looking up. And on the third morning, the mountain disappears into a cloud. Thunder. Lightning. A trumpet blast that keeps getting louder. Smoke rising off the top like a furnace. The ground shaking under their feet. And everyone in the camp trembles.
screen: `THREE MONTHS OUT.` → `THE MOUNTAIN OF THE BUSH.` → `THUNDER, SMOKE, A TRUMPET.`

segments.voice: Before the thunder, there's a message, and it comes first. God tells Moses to say to the people: you've seen what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. Deuteronomy later fills in that picture: an eagle stirring up her nest, spreading her wings, catching her young and carrying them. Not a cage. A carrying. Second, the promise. If you keep my covenant, God says, you'll be my own treasured possession among all the peoples, for all the earth is mine. The Hebrew word is segullah. It's the word a king used for his private treasure, the things that were personally his. And then: you'll be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people answer together: all that the Lord has spoken, we will do. Third, the preparation. Three days to get ready. Wash your clothes. Don't touch the mountain. Then the cloud comes down, and the people stand back trembling while Moses goes up into it. Fourth, how Catholics hear it. Peter's first letter takes these very words and gives them to the baptized: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people." The Church calls this the common priesthood of all the faithful: every baptized person is part of a people that belongs to God and offers the world back to God. And Catholics notice another echo. Jewish tradition came to link the feast of Shavuot, fifty days after Passover, with the giving of the law at Sinai. On that same feast, Pentecost, the Spirit came down on the apostles with wind, fire and a sound from heaven.
screen: `I CARRIED YOU ON EAGLES' WINGS.` · `SEGULLAH: MY OWN TREASURE.` · `THREE DAYS, THEN THE CLOUD.` · `A KINGLY PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a mountain in a cloud. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes if that helps. See a mountain, rough and enormous, its top wrapped in a thick cloud you can't see into. Hear the wind. Feel the ground under you, solid, and then just slightly trembling. You're at the foot, with thousands of others, not at the top. That's fine. The people stood at the foot too. Let yourself feel small in front of something enormous and alive. If you pray, you can stay there in silence before God. If you don't, simply stay with the picture, and notice the awe. The bell holds the time.
Sinai. The mountain of the burning bush, wrapped in cloud and thunder, where God named a rescued people his own. Today's word.
Your line: a people of his own. Today, look at the people around you at work or on the street, and see each one as somebody's treasure. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

378.title: The ten words (Exodus 20:1–17)
378.hook: I am the Lord thy God who brought thee out: freedom comes before the rules
378.howItsDone: Many Catholics examine their conscience before confession by going through the Ten Commandments one at a time, following the numbering found in the Catechism, which traces back to Saint Augustine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sinai: thunder, smoke, a trumpet, and a people told they were God's own treasure. Your line was a people of his own. This week ran from the lamb through the sea, Miriam's drum, manna and Moses's tired arms, to the mountain. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

Ask most people to recite the Ten Commandments and they'll start with thou shalt not, and get through four or five before they stall. Almost nobody starts where the text starts. Because the first thing God says from the mountain isn't a rule at all. It's a sentence about the past. A reminder of who's speaking, and what that speaker has already done. Before a single command, there's an introduction. And Exodus itself doesn't call them commandments. It calls them the ten words.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT... AND THEN?` → `IT DOESN'T START WITH A RULE.` → `THE TEN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line, as the Douay-Rheims has it: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." Then, and only then: "Thou shalt not have strange gods before me." The order matters. God doesn't say, keep these rules and I'll free you. God says, I already freed you. Now here's how free people live. The commandments are a description of freedom, not the price of it. Second, the name. In Hebrew they're the aseret ha-devarim, the ten words or ten sayings; the Greek gave us Decalogue, from the same idea. Third, the counting. The text has more than ten sentences, so traditions divide them differently. Catholics and Lutherans follow a division that goes back to Saint Augustine: no other gods and no carved images make one commandment, and coveting a neighbor's wife and coveting his goods make two. Orthodox and most other Protestant churches count the images as a separate commandment and the coveting as one. In Jewish tradition the first word is the opening line itself, I am the Lord thy God. Same text, different ways of counting it, and nobody's list is missing anything. Fourth, the shape. Love of God comes first, then the rest turns to people: parents, life, marriage, property, truth, desire. The Catechism says the ten words are meant to be read inside the story of the Exodus: they mark out the life of a people set free. Slaves had no Sabbath. Free people get one, by command.
screen: `I BROUGHT THEE OUT. THEN: THE LAW.` · `ASERET HA-DEVARIM: TEN WORDS.` · `ONE TEXT, DIFFERENT WAYS TO COUNT.` · `GOD FIRST, THEN NEIGHBOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the commandments as gifts. Settle, and breathe. Pick one commandment, whichever comes to mind first. Now turn it around. Instead of hearing it as a fence, hear it as a gift to someone. Thou shalt not steal is a gift to your neighbor: their things are safe with you. Keep holy the Sabbath is a gift to you: one day you don't have to produce anything. Honor your father and mother is a gift to people who are getting old. Try it with yours. If you pray, you can thank God for that one gift. If you don't, just notice who it protects. The bell holds the time.
The ten words. The Bible's own name for the commandments given at Sinai, which begin not with a rule but with a rescue. Today's word.
Your line: freedom first, then the law. Today, when a rule chafes, ask what freedom it's protecting, for you or for someone else. Day three hundred seventy-eight.
